extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical rhetoric; writers and readers interested in prose/style theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts classical (Aristotelian/Peripatetic) principles for good prose style as discussed in Longinus, Demetrius, and allied authorities — focusing on clearness, decorum/fitness, ornament, and the four types/forms of style. Useful for writers learning how to choose diction, rhythm, and force appropriate to rhetorical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit words to the dignity of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Suit the words to the dignity of the subject and thus imitate Nature’ — choose diction that matches the subject's dignity; elevated subjects require elevated diction, low subjects require correspondingly plain diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that in elevated passages one must avoid recourse to sordid or contemptible words except under extreme necessity; Nature hides dishonourable parts, and style should mirror that concealment. This principle is presented as a primary check on inappropriate vocabulary in lofty discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid untimely or incongruous details in description
rubrics_metrics.description: The untimely introduction of incongruous specifics (e.g., flashy riches in an otherwise dignified scene) constitutes a flaw in description and brands it with infamy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example guidance from the text: rather than abruptly listing 'silver, pavilions of solid gold, and the drinking cups,' the author suggests alternatives that preserve register — e.g., 'camels and a multitude of baggage animals laden with all that serves the luxury and pleasure of the table,' or 'heaps of every kind of grain and of all known aids to cookery and good living,' or 'all the dainties known to caterers and cooks.' The point: match specificity and level of detail to overall tone; avoid jarring particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal vulgar/obscene or dishonourable details (backgrounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature did not place in full view our dishonourable parts; likewise, writers should push sordid or indelicate material to the furthest background to preserve the beauty of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use backgrounding and selective disclosure rather than explicit exposure of ignoble matters; reserve explicitness only under extreme necessity. The passage cites Xenophon as support for placing such channels 'into the furthest background.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness (clarity) as the primary essential
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Style to be good must be clear’ — speech or writing must convey a plain meaning; without clarity speech fails to perform its function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle and Demetrius both emphasize clarity as the foremost requisite. Demetrius 'enjoins clearness, giving hints for its attainment' (see cited §§190–203). Practices that obscure meaning (overly ornate diction, convoluted syntax) should be avoided or subordinated to perspicuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness / appropriateness (decorum; good taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style must be appropriate to its subject and purpose, avoiding both meanness and undue elevation; appropriateness (fitness) is governed by good taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle: avoid poetic language in prose when inappropriate. The notion of 7d mpérov (decorum/fitness) underlies both clearness and the avoidance of extremes. Good taste restrains ornament and selects diction and rhythm that fit the subject-matter and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit ornament; prefer plain style for clearness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament is distrusted because it tends to obscure meaning; a plain style best secures clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle and Demetrius warn that ornament can lead to fine writing that sacrifices function. Use ornament sparingly and only where it serves clarity or appropriateness; in prose, restraint is preferable to flamboyance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bathos and bombast
rubrics_metrics.description: Bathos (inappropriate descent into triviality) and bombast (inflated, pompous diction) are faults to be pilloried and avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demetrius explicitly attacks bathos and bombast (cited §§114, 121, 304). The practical application is to guard against slips from the lofty into the ridiculous and against unwarranted grandeur that collapses into absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend ordinary and unusual words; cultivate rhythm and appropriateness to create agreeableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreeableness or magnificence of style arises from the good blending of ordinary and unusual words, from rhythm, and from persuasiveness that springs from appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This offers constructive levers: (1) mix familiar and striking diction thoughtfully; (2) attend to sentence rhythm (periodic shaping); (3) ensure persuasive force grows organically from fitness of expression. These elements together produce ‘agreeable’ or ‘magnificent’ style as described by commentators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid both prolixity and excessive curtness; seek the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: If prose is prolix it is not clear; if it is too curt it is not clear — the middle way (the moderate length/pace) suits best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity must be subordinated to clearness; do not compress expression to the point of obscurity nor expand it to the point of tedium. Use the level of expansion appropriate to the subject and the reader's need for comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style type to rhetorical aim (moving, pleasing, proving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose among stylistic characters/types in accordance with the rhetorical purpose — e.g., styles aimed at moving, pleasing, or proving require different emphases and techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demetrius (drawing on tradition) treats multiple 'types' of style (the fourfold framework) and notes that masters like Demosthenes command different styles for different ends; so select grand/forcible diction to move, a more elegant/smooth style to please, and a restrained/clear style to prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of force (forcible/forcible style) as an advanced aim
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'forcible' or powerful style (devdny / forcible xapaxrip) is a distinct type emphasizing concentrated force and mastery; it is exemplified by Demosthenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demetrius treats forcible style as separable from mere agreeableness; practitioners seeking overpowering effect should cultivate concentrated intensity, but must distinguish genuine force from mere rhetorical artifice. Hermogenes' varieties of force (appearing as, being, seeming) caution against imitation without substance.
